**The Physics of Ordinary Light**

There's a particular hour—late afternoon in autumn—when sunlight comes in at such a low angle that it turns every room into a planetarium of dust. The motes drift like tiny planets, each one catching light that left the sun eight minutes ago. It's easy to forget that light is a traveler. We flip a switch and assume illumination is instantaneous, a property of rooms rather than a thing arriving from elsewhere.

But everything we see is news. The moon we admire tonight is a report filed 1.3 seconds late. The nearest star's twinkle is years old. When you look at the Andromeda galaxy—visible, faintly, from a dark enough field—you're seeing something so ancient that dinosaurs had not yet evolved when those photons began their journey.

I love that seeing is a kind of time travel available to everyone, no equipment required. Every glance across space is also a glance backward through time. Right now, light is arriving somewhere that departed before anything recognizable as human existed.

And yet the same physics governs the dust mote drifting past your window. Scale doesn't change the rules; it only changes our attention. A child blowing dandelion seeds is running the same experiment as an astronomer measuring redshift—releasing something small into forces too vast to see.

Maybe attention is the real instrument. Telescopes help, equations help, but the essential act is older than both: pausing long enough to notice that the universe has been broadcasting all along. The signal never stopped. The only question is whether anyone is listening—or looking up.
